extracted.intended_audience: historians and philosophers of science, practicing scientists and advanced students interested in the nature of scientific change and paradigm shifts
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and evaluate the features, causes, and consequences of scientific revolutions (paradigm shifts), including how paradigms change what counts as facts, laws, concepts, and acceptable tests. The material is aimed at scholars assessing historical episodes or philosophical accounts of paradigm change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigm-change criterion: operations retain form but change significance
rubrics_metrics.description: One and the same laboratory operation or manipulation can, when attached to a different paradigm, become an index to a quite different aspect of nature’s regularity; alternatively the old manipulation in its new role may yield different concrete results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: eighteenth-century chemical manipulations (guided by affinity theory) and those same manipulations after Dalton’s atomic paradigm — identical procedures but different interpretations and sometimes different measured results. When evaluating historical scientific practice, look for cases where identical techniques are reinterpreted or produce new results after a paradigmatic shift.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law-emergence depends on paradigm
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain generalizations or ‘laws’ (e.g., the law of fixed proportions) could not have been produced by experiment under the assumptions of the preceding paradigm; they become possible or meaningful only after a paradigmatic reconceptualization of the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Under affinity theory, solutions were viewed as compounds and the regularities like fixed proportions were not generalizable; Dalton’s paradigm made such a law explicable and constitutive. In evaluating claims of discovery, check whether the purported law required a prior conceptual shift to be articulable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textbook-truncation/rewriting effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Textbooks, popularizations, and philosophic accounts written after a revolution record the stable outcome of the revolution and thus typically truncate, distort, or omit the historical process by which the new paradigm was recognized and accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textbooks aim to teach the vocabulary and syntax of the current scientific language and often provide only selected bits of history that make past work appear continuous with the present paradigm. When using textbooks as historical evidence, be cautious: they are pedagogic vehicles that disguise the role and even existence of revolutions and must be rewritten after revolutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concepts acquire scientific content only within paradigm-linked practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbal definitions of scientific concepts (e.g., 'element') have little scientific content by themselves; concepts gain full significance only when related to other scientific concepts, manipulative procedures, and paradigm applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Boyle’s verbal 'definition' of element resembled later textbook formulas but did not by itself have the scientific meaning it later acquired through changes in practice (Lavoisier, etc.). Therefore, evaluations of conceptual invention should examine the surrounding experimental and theoretical context, not only verbal definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of successful revolutionary innovators
rubrics_metrics.description: New candidates for paradigm emerge in the minds of a few individuals whose attention has intensely concentrated upon crisis-provoking problems and who are often young or new enough to be less committed to the old paradigm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These individuals are able to see science and the world differently. In historical or sociological analysis, assess whether proponents of a new paradigm displayed intense focus on anomalies/crisis problems and relative freedom from entrenched commitments to the predecessor paradigm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradigm-testing is comparative and historically situated
rubrics_metrics.description: Testing of paradigms occurs not by neutral comparison of a single paradigm with nature but as part of competition between rival paradigms for the allegiance of the scientific community; paradigm-testing typically follows a period of crisis and the emergence of an alternative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect paradigm-testing to be a straightforward, context-free series of neutral experiments. Instead, evaluate how competing paradigms account for existing evidence, how each frames problems, and how the community’s allegiance shifts in response to comparative performance and problem-solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of probabilistic/neutral verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Probabilistic verification theories that require construction of all possible alternate tests or theories presuppose a neutral observation-language; such neutral, paradigm-free construction is impossible, so verification proceeds from within particular paradigm traditions and selects among the actual historical alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying probabilistic or justificatory frameworks, recognize that any assessment of a theory’s probability is constrained by the conceptual and observational resources available within particular paradigms; do not assume access to all conceivable tests or theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revolution can change empirical data and measurements
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptance of a new paradigm can lead to changes in the very numerical data or their presentation (e.g., chemists changed how they recorded compositions and atomic weights), so that after a revolution scientists 'work in a different world.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: After Dalton’s paradigm, chemists reported combining ratios (1.3 or 2.6 weights of oxygen per weight of carbon) rather than percentages, making simple ratios visually salient. Historical evaluation should consider not only reinterpretation but also how measurement practices and recorded data themselves change with paradigms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance depends on problem-solving power, assimilation, and fruitfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: A new paradigm convinces the community when it has implications wider and more important than mere definitional changes: it should reveal new regularities, assimilate prior results, suggest new experiments, and reorganize practice to be more fruitful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Dalton’s paradigm allowed assimilation of Richter’s work, suggested Gay-Lussac’s volume experiments, and changed chemical practice. In appraising a candidate paradigm, weigh its explanatory breadth, ability to integrate prior findings, and the new research trajectories it enables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textbook presentation creates illusion of piecemeal cumulative progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Because textbooks present the elements of current normal science as separate items arranged seriatim, they foster the impression that science advanced by piecemeal discovery and cumulative addition, whereas many contemporary puzzles only arise after a revolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reconstructing scientific development, beware narratives that treat facts and theories as independently discovered pieces that were always sought; instead, investigate how revolutions reformulate problems and jointly produce new facts and theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical attributions in pedagogic texts can misrepresent origins
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributions in textbooks (e.g., crediting Boyle with inventing the modern concept of element) often misrepresent the historical role of individuals; such attributions can obscure that what matters is how concepts were transformed in relation to practice across multiple revolutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Boyle’s 'definition' echoed earlier tradition and he argued differently in context; the modern concept of 'element' required later revolutions (Lavoisier). Use primary sources and contextual analysis rather than textbook attributions when tracing conceptual origins.
